name: Light Danube Green
lede: Light Danube Green is a muted, slightly blue-leaning green named for the Danube, the river that crosses central and southeastern Europe, and recorded as a color standard since at least 1912.

sections.title: A river's name
sections.body:
The Danube runs some 2,850 kilometers from Germany's Black Forest to the Black Sea, through or beside ten countries, more than any other river on Earth [3]. Ridgway's 1912 color standards give this green on plate XXXII, hue 35 double-prime, tone k, a scan of an aged printed plate and so only approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 files the same swatch, block 145, as a moderate green, and gives it the Munsell notation 7.1G 4.4/3.8 [1].

Its nearest named neighbors in our library are Deep Jade and Diamine Green, both about 2.5 units away, then Hooker's Green at 2.6 [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[diamine-green]], [[deep-jade]] and [[hooker-s-green]], at 2.5, 2.5 and 2.6 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Light Danube Green covers at least five percent of the canvas in 92 works, under half of one percent [2]. The earliest dated example is Hans Memling's 1480 portrait of an unknown man with a letter, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It peaks in the 1910s, in 9 of 523 paintings, more than four times the archive's overall rate for that decade [2]. Gustave Caillebotte carries it in three of his twenty-two paintings here and Vincent van Gogh in six of forty-nine, both well above the baseline, and French paintings as a group carry it three times the baseline rate [2]. It shares a canvas with [[viridian]] far more than chance, thirty-seven times the baseline [2]. As with every number here, this is a screen-color match on photographed, varnished canvases, not a pigment test [2].
